extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and researchers in mathematics education (particularly those interested in undergraduate/advanced undergraduate student development)
extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative exploration and preliminary rubric-like characterization of 'mathematical maturity' as used by mathematicians about advanced undergraduate students, drawing on interviews and prior literature. Produces three high-level components and multiple concrete indicators frequently invoked by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways of Thinking about Mathematics (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A category of attributes describing how a student thinks about mathematics rather than discrete skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page groups several indicators under this heading (see specific items below). These capture meta-cognitive and epistemic dispositions toward the subject rather than procedure-level competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Having a holistic view of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed by participants as an aspect of 'ways of thinking'—seeing mathematics as an interconnected whole rather than isolated procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (M3): the ability to 'read the story and understand the moral' rather than only seeing isolated facts (e.g., beyond 'there are infinitely many primes' to the deeper point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Being accepting of multiple representations and changing definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness and ability to work with multiple representations and to accept that definitions may change depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included under 'ways of thinking' as a sign of flexibility in understanding mathematical objects and their descriptions; indicates tolerance for abstraction and re-formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Having autonomy or agency over their own learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students take responsibility for their learning, direct their own study, and exercise independent judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a dispositional indicator—mathematically mature students show self-directed learning rather than reliance on external authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Intuition (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A category capturing the semi-conscious/problem-solving sense mathematicians use: hunches, judgments about methods and results, and quick pattern synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper ties this to literature (Feferman, Fischbein, Tall) which describe intuition as insight/illumination, unconscious organization/synthesis, and the global amalgam of local cognitive processes. Practitioners view intuition as necessary but offer little concrete instruction on how to develop it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing what to do with problems
rubrics_metrics.description: An intuitive sense of appropriate approaches or next steps when faced with a mathematical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by interviewees under 'mathematical intuition'—the ability to decide promising methods or problem approaches without only following rote procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing the crux of an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to identify the central difficulty or key step in a proof or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees report this as an intuition-based skill—recognizing which piece of an argument carries the real content or challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing if a solution makes sense
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal check or judgment that a proposed solution is plausible or consistent with expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of intuition: being able to evaluate the plausibility of results and detect when a solution is likely erroneous or superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comfort with and Competence in Mathematics (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A category emphasizing concrete skills and fluency: technical competence, communicative ability, abstraction, and self-monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category contains several concrete indicators used by mathematicians to identify maturity (see specific items below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to absorb and use definitions and theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility with learning, internalizing, and correctly applying formal definitions and theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a necessary skill for advanced work—being able to 'absorb' formal material and deploy it appropriately in new contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to effectively communicate mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in expressing intuitive ideas using sensible notation and words so that ideas are understandable across different levels of mathematical comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote (M5): 'Being able to take an intuitive idea and express it using a sensible notation, and yeah, putting it into words in a sense.' Interviewees stressed importance of communicating both one's own ideas and understanding others' explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to abstract and make connections across topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to see and formulate useful abstractions and to connect concepts across different mathematical areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M3 emphasized 'the ability to abstract in a useful way'—seeing the bigger picture and motivation behind proofs rather than only surface details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to self-assess, validate, and reconstruct arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in critically evaluating one's work, validating correctness, and reworking/reconstructing arguments when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an indicator of maturity: the student can internal-check proofs and rebuild arguments, not just accept or reproduce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steen's 'marks of maturity' / ability-based criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical list of abilities frequently cited as marks of mathematical maturity: ability to abstract; ability to synthesize; use and interpret mathematical notation; generalize; perceive patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Steen (1983): these are abilities most mathematicians instantly recognize as components of maturity. The paper treats them as prior expert-opinion criteria that informed the interview coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonavailing mathematical beliefs (negative indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs identified in the literature that negatively influence mathematical learning and are considered nonindicators or counter-signs of maturity: (1) mathematical knowledge is unchanging; (2) the goal in mathematics is to find the correct answer; (3) knowledge is delivered by an authority; (4) mathematical ability is innate; (5) components of mathematical knowledge are unrelated; (6) students cannot construct knowledge themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Muis (2004) synthesis—these epistemological beliefs are associated with poorer learning outcomes. The paper highlights them as beliefs to identify and change, not as signs of maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical intuition (literature definitions and characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature-derived characterizations of intuition: Feferman—'insight or illumination' and 'hunches' about profitable problems/methods; Fischbein—unconscious ability to organize, synthesize experience, guess beyond facts; Tall—'global amalgam of local processes' selectively stimulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characterizations inform the study's interpretation of interview statements about intuition; they emphasize unconscious/semi-conscious synthesis, problem-selection hunches, and rapid organization of prior experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tao's three-stage developmental framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A developmental account: pre-rigorous stage (informal), rigorous stage (precise/formal), and post-rigorous stage (return to informed intuition supported by rigorous foundations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao's framework is presented as an explanatory model for how mathematical maturity might develop over time and what educators might expect across stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thurston's components for mathematical thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects Thurston suggested are important for mathematical thinking: human language, visual/spatial sense, logic/deduction, intuition/association/metaphor, stimulus-response, and process/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the literature review to argue maturity involves diverse cognitive resources, not just formal logic; suggests multiple modes of reasoning should be fostered.
